subject: The measured storage and memory cost of faster HTML opening in Terminal Delight, and a bounded cache strategy for many panes.
reader: Parker uses Terminal Delight with 30 to 50 agent panes and asks whether caching only nine recent panes avoids excessive overhead. He wants measured costs and a clear recommendation.

sections.heading: What Faster Opening Costs
sections.text: To speed up HTML opening across 30–50 Terminal Delight panes, save the finished page pictures on disk. The disk cache currently holds 58 rendered versions in 229 MiB. Keeping nine browser pages alive used 1.93 GiB of RAM.

sections.heading: 01 Stored Artifacts
sections.text:
Declaring an artifact stores its link and label; it does not render the page. The original HTML stays where its author saved it. Completed renders live in the shared cache below, with a 256 MiB budget across panes and windows . 

 /home/parker/.cache/terminal-delight/pages/ 
 01 · Existing Disk Cache 

 The existing disk budget already holds dozens of rendered versions. Measured census: 58 renders and six media entries. Median render 3.3 MiB; largest 22.2 MiB. Different sizes or revisions can occupy separate entries. Census . 

The cache holds compressed page pictures and layout data. Eviction removes the least recently used entries after storage, so temporary writes can exceed the budget. Linux may also cache these files in reclaimable RAM.

sections.heading: 02 Open Browser Pages
sections.text:
Fresh rendering opens a page in TD’s shared Chromium process. I retained nine pages using the real renderer, then closed them. The faster Vulkan mode reduced RAM but used additional graphics memory. 
 02 · Closing Pages Releases Most of the Cost 

 Nine live browser pages are an expensive cache. RAM is measured across Chromium’s processes with shared memory apportioned once. Graphics memory is reported separately by the NVIDIA driver. Closing every page leaves the shared browser running; shutdown released all measured browser memory. Method and raw evidence . 

Three ordinary glass briefs, each opened three times, at 968 × 1400 CSS pixels and scale 1.6. One resource run per mode. The source closes the browser after five minutes without an engine call. Temporary profiles normally live under /run/user/1000/terminal-delight/ ; the experiment’s profile files occupied about 2.6 MiB in the default run.

sections.heading: 03 Thirty to Fifty Panes
sections.text:
TD keeps its own compressed pictures and decoded pixels while a document remains open, including when its pane is hidden. For the nine sampled views, those add 48 MiB of PNGs and 281 MiB of decoded pixel data . Native display textures cost extra; their actual driver allocation was not measured. 
 03 · Growth Without Releasing Pages 
 | 
 | Open documents | Browser RAM | Decoded pixels 
 | 9 · measured browser | 1.93 GiB | 281 MiB 
 | 30 · estimate | 6.1 GiB | 936 MiB 
 | 50 · estimate | 10.0 GiB | 1,560 MiB 

 Keeping many rendered documents alive can cost gigabytes. The 30/50 rows extrapolate the measured nine-page mix; they are not stress-test results. Pixel counts come from image dimensions and TD’s retention rule. Smaller panes cost less. These rows describe opened documents before browser idle shutdown, not links sitting on the artifact rail. sections.heading: 04 Recommended Strategy
sections.text:
Use the nine most recently visited panes to rank preparation , beginning with the focused pane’s newest artifact. Run one cancellable job at a time, close its browser page when capture finishes, and retain the completed disk snapshot. Release decoded images from hidden documents while preserving notes and scroll position. 
 04 · Bound the Expensive Work 

 Recency chooses the work; byte budgets limit storage. Proposed policy, unimplemented. Avoid eagerly rendering all nine candidates. Completed cache reads previously took 1–6 ms, so a second cache of PNGs pinned in RAM has little demonstrated benefit. Preparation still consumes CPU/GPU time and needs cancellation and a measured memory ceiling. 

 The next check is how quickly a hidden document reopens after its images are released. The revised plan tests that with 9, 30 and 50 panes before rollout. It keeps the 200–300 ms ambition for prepared opens. The earlier speed measurements also show why Vulkan’s first-open delay needs repair. 

These are proposed changes. The application still behaves as before; the combined implementation plan awaits approval.
